entries.clue: Mess up drink request for the most part (6)

indicatorNotes.for the most part: For the most part is most of a thing but not all of it, so the word it follows arrives one letter short at the tail.

blocks.note: rum is the spirit the crossword reaches for first
a request is a PLEA, and only the most of it is being asked for

annotation.surface: Getting a drinks order mostly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: A plea is a request in the formal sense - entering a plea, a plea for calm - which is the step the letters skip over. 'For the most part' nearly always takes the final letter off rather than the first.
annotation.definitionFit: To rumple a shirt or a bed is to leave it creased and out of order, which is to mess it up.

entries.clue: So involved a decision for intellectuals, says Cockney (2,2,3,8)

indicatorNotes.says Cockney: A Cockney speaker drops the aitch from the front of a word, so what follows is to be heard in that accent rather than read as it is printed.

blocks.note: highbrows are the intellectuals, and a matter left up to them is their decision; with the aitch gone the phrase is said exactly like the answer

annotation.surface: A Cockney saying some knotty choice ought to be left to the clever people.
annotation.walkthrough: Leaving a matter 'up to' someone makes it their decision, and highbrows are the intellectuals. Cockney speech drops the aitch that begins a word, a habit setters lean on whenever a single H stands between two real phrases.
annotation.definitionFit: To be up to the eyebrows in something is to be immersed past any chance of standing back, which is what 'so involved' describes.

entries.clue: Horned god, wicked one that'll cure all (7)

blocks.note: Pan, the Greek god drawn with a goat's horns and legs
ace as praise means excellent, the slang sense wicked also carries
the indefinite article stands in for one

annotation.surface: A horned god and some wicked character who will apparently heal anything.
annotation.walkthrough: Pan is the crossword's standard horned god, goat-legged and pipe-playing. 'Wicked' is the playground compliment rather than the moral judgement, which is the only reading that lets it mean ACE.
annotation.definitionFit: A cure-all is the single remedy claimed to answer every ailment, and panacea is the older name for exactly that claim.

entries.clue: Mysterious giant mice exploding (9)

indicatorNotes.exploding: Something exploding scatters its parts across the floor, and scattered letters have to be gathered back in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: Enormous mice detonating.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is three words, so the letter count settles it early: 'giant mice' runs to exactly nine. Picturing rodents blowing up is the only reason those two words are standing next to each other.
annotation.definitionFit: Something enigmatic resists explanation and invites guessing, which is the ordinary force of mysterious.

entries.clue: Step? Not half! Travel ... travel with long steps (6)

indicatorNotes.Not half: Not half denies you the whole of the word before it, leaving the front two letters of a four-letter one.

blocks.note: the front half of STEP
to ride is to travel, on a horse or in a car

annotation.surface: A walker scoffing at the idea of a single step and setting off to travel instead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is the British exclamation meaning very much so, which is the reverse of the instruction it is carrying. The row of dots is typography rather than wordplay - it lets one verb serve the clue twice.
annotation.definitionFit: To stride is to walk with unusually long paces, so the definition spells out the manner the verb already carries.

entries.clue: Barber is, we're told, very nearly vertical? (5)

indicatorNotes.we're told: What we are told is what we hear rather than what we read, so the words that follow supply a sound and the answer is spelt another way.

blocks.note: a sheer drop is one that falls away almost perpendicular, and the two spellings are said identically

annotation.surface: Word has it that a barber stands very nearly upright.
annotation.walkthrough: Take 'Barber' as a verb rather than the man in the shop: to barber somebody is to cut their hair. SHEAR and SHEER have separate jobs and one sound, which is all the clue needs.
annotation.definitionFit: To barber is to cut hair, and to shear is to cut hair or wool close to the skin - the same action in the same grammatical slot.

entries.clue: Gives another polish to snubs (7)

blocks.note: buffing is polishing, and RE- on the front makes it a second go over the same surface
the everyday sense, turning a person or an offer away sharply

annotation.surface: Someone bringing a set of snubs up to a shine again.
annotation.walkthrough: A buff is a polish - the verb survives in 'buffed up' - and RE- in front of it makes a repeat. The setter's whole trick is withholding the hyphen that would give that reading away.
annotation.definitionFit: Buff again and the shine comes back; and to rebuff a person is to turn them away coldly, the same seven letters read as one word.

entries.clue: Prostrate, eyes closed: what'll keep nobleman warm in bed? (4,3,3,5)

annotation.definition2: what'll keep nobleman warm in bed?
annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is not a dictionary sense: the phrase is being re-read word by word as bedding bought for a nobleman, which is why it arrives as a question rather than a synonym.

blocks.note: the boxing sense - flat on the canvas while the referee counts over you

blocks.clueFragment: what'll keep nobleman warm in bed?
blocks.note: read as a shopping list instead: duvet down, bought for a count

annotation.surface: Someone laid out flat with eyes shut, and the question of what warms a nobleman's bed.
annotation.walkthrough: Down is the soft under-feather that fills a duvet, and a count is a nobleman ranking below a marquess. Left alone, the phrase means only what the referee's count of ten means to a fighter on the canvas.
annotation.definitionFit: A fighter down for the count lies stretched out and not getting up; read word by word, the same phrase names duvet down bought for a count.

entries.clue: Recovered from intense blow, sporting affliction (6,5)

indicatorNotes.Recovered: Recovered here is re-covered, as a chair is recovered: given a fresh covering, so the letters come back arranged another way.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: Someone who has got over a heavy punch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recovered from' is the everyday phrase for getting better and also the instruction to rearrange. Tennis elbow comes from repeating a stroke rather than from any punch, so the injury in the surface is the wrong injury.
annotation.definitionFit: Tennis elbow is the inflamed tendon racket players pick up from repeated strokes, a complaint named after the sport that causes it.

entries.clue: Further allusion regularly unnecessary (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly unnecessary: Letters called regularly unnecessary are the ones thrown out at a fixed interval, so every second letter of the word beside it goes.

blocks.note: keeping the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of ALLUSION

annotation.surface: A further mention being dismissed as routinely pointless.
annotation.walkthrough: An eight-letter word can only yield four by this route, and the enumeration confirms that before you have looked. 'Allusion' is placed to read as the thing being called unnecessary, which is what stops it looking like raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: Further in the sense of in addition - 'further, the bill is unpaid' - is the slot ALSO would fill.

entries.clue: Cut string taken from dachshund (4)

indicatorNotes.string taken from: A string is an unbroken run of letters, and one taken from a word comes out of it whole and in the order it was lying.

blocks.note: dacHSHUNd: the fifth to eighth letters, sitting together

annotation.surface: A length of string cut off a dachshund.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' is the social sense: to cut someone is to walk past as though they were not there. Dachshund is German for badger dog, which is why an English clue can hide so unlikely a run of letters in it.
annotation.definitionFit: To cut a person is to ignore them on purpose, the deliberate snub that SHUN names.

entries.clue: Meet up with Carol - she's not on time (9)

annotation.definitionNote: A latecomer is a person, while 'she's not on time' is a statement about one; the setter names the noun by describing the woman it applies to.

indicatorNotes.up: Up as in mixed up: the letters beside it are not staying in the order they were printed.

blocks.note: four of the nine letters to be rearranged
the other five, a woman's name on the surface

annotation.surface: Arranging to meet Carol, who never turns up punctually.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Meet up with' is one idiom in the surface, which is exactly what hides the instruction sitting in the middle of it. Carol stays a name right up until you need her five letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A latecomer is whoever arrives after the appointed hour, so the clue names the person by the fault.

entries.clue: Proportion's half, if that's taking 50% (5)

indicatorNotes.taking 50%: Taking 50% says how much of the words beside it you keep - five letters out of ten - and they come away in the order they were printed.

blocks.note: run the words together and halFIFTHat carries the answer straight through its middle

annotation.surface: Someone calling a share barely half, if that.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half, if that' is ordinary English hedging - a shade under fifty per cent - which is why it never looks like material to work on. A fifth is twenty per cent, so the arithmetic on the surface was never going to add up.
annotation.definitionFit: A fifth is one part in five, which is a proportion in the plain sense of a share of a whole.

entries.clue: Deliveries, one hundred tons: as ham this'll do? (7)

blocks.note: an over is the set of six deliveries a cricket bowler sends down from one end
the article standing for one
C is the Roman hundred
t is the standard short form for tons

annotation.surface: Deliveries weighed out by the hundred tons, and a verdict that this much ham will serve.
annotation.walkthrough: Cricket's over is six deliveries bowled from one end, and it is the piece a solver outside Britain is least likely to hold. A ham actor is named from ham fat, the grease nineteenth-century players used to take off their make-up.
annotation.definitionFit: To ham is to play a part far too broadly, which is what OVERACT says in plainer words.

entries.clue: Alas, sadly as an alternative, admitted Everyman ultimately no-hoper (4-3)

indicatorNotes.sadly: Sadly colours the word beside it as something gone wrong, and letters gone wrong are letters out of their proper order.
indicatorNotes.admitted: To admit something is to let it in, so the letter named next joins the pile being rearranged rather than standing outside it.

blocks.note: four of the seven letters
or is the word that offers an alternative
the last letter of Everyman

annotation.surface: Everyman regretfully owning up to being the substitute who got let in at the last.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his own puzzles, so 'Everyman ultimately' points at the final letter of the setter's name rather than at anybody in the race. A race result lists the unplaced horses under the words 'also ran'.
annotation.definitionFit: The unplaced horses in a printed race result appear under 'also ran', and the phrase transferred to any competitor with no chance of winning.

entries.clue: Source of music that's long - and high! (9)

annotation.definition: Source of music that's long - and high!

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a note held on and on at the top of the register

blocks.clueFragment: Source of music that's long - and high!
blocks.note: the reading meant: an instrument that really is several metres long, played high up in the mountains

annotation.surface: A musical note that goes on and on at the top of the register.
annotation.walkthrough: An alpenhorn is the wooden tube, three or four metres of it, that Swiss herdsmen sound across valleys. Both 'long' and 'high' have to be taken physically, and the exclamation mark is the only warning that they have changed sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Every part of the clue reads straight of the instrument: the alpenhorn makes music, it is literally long, and it belongs high in the Alps.

entries.clue: Primarily cumbersomely rambling; you piece together its components - like this? (7)

indicatorNotes.Primarily: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is wanted.

blocks.clueFragment: cumbersomely rambling; you piece together its components
blocks.note: the seven opening letters, in the order printed

annotation.surface: An awkward, rambling instruction to build something out of its parts.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is describing his own clue while writing it: 'you piece together its components' is both the surface and the thing a solver is doing. Seven words in the run, seven letters in the light.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Like this' points at the clue it sits in, and a clue put together this way is a cryptic one.

entries.clue: Perhaps Jack's a funny fellow (4)

blocks.note: the jack is one of the four court ranks in a pack, and perhaps warns that an example is standing in for the whole class
old British slang for a wag, the sort who keeps a room laughing

annotation.surface: Jack turning out to be an amusing sort of chap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the setter's flag for definition by example - a jack is a card, but a card need not be a jack. Calling a joker a card is Edwardian slang that now survives mostly in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: The jack is one of the pack, so 'perhaps' lets the example stand for the kind; and a funny fellow is a card in old British slang.

entries.clue: Spooner's ridden at speed for quantity of ale (7)

indicatorNotes.Spooner's: Spooner is the Oxford don remembered for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so the phrase named next has its first sounds exchanged.

blocks.note: a horse ridden at speed has cantered; exchange the opening sounds of CAN and TERED and what comes out is said like the answer

annotation.surface: Spooner riding hard in return for a pint.
annotation.walkthrough: William Spooner was the warden of New College whose tongue kept swapping the fronts of words, and crosswords have kept his name for the device ever since. A tankard is the handled pewter or pottery mug British pubs poured beer into.
annotation.definitionFit: A tankard holds about a pint, and British usage lets the mug's name stand for the measure of ale inside it.

entries.clue: Bags of salt in small amounts (7)

blocks.note: to bag something is to take it, and to pinch it is the same theft in more childish words
the cook's pinch, as much as thumb and forefinger will grip

annotation.surface: Salt being bagged up in small quantities.
annotation.walkthrough: Bags and pinches are both playground words for helping yourself to what is not yours, and both are verbs in the first reading. The other half is a kitchen measure with no fixed size at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Bags -> PINCHES: both mean takes without asking; salt in small amounts -> PINCHES: a pinch is the smallest measure a cook uses, as much as two fingers hold.

entries.clue: Succeed in, with Rev's support, getting help posting notices (4,3)

indicatorNotes.support: What supports a thing sits underneath it, and underneath in a down entry means the letters that come second.

blocks.note: to nail something is to succeed at it outright
to gun an engine is to rev it hard

annotation.surface: A vicar lending a hand with the parish noticeboard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rev' is the clergyman on the surface and the accelerator underneath, which is the whole joke of the sentence. Support means below in a down entry, so the revving is the half that goes second.
annotation.definitionFit: A nail gun drives fixings into wood at a squeeze of the trigger, which is exactly the help you would want for putting notices up.

entries.clue: Small fuss: flipped over drink (non-alcoholic) (4)

indicatorNotes.flipped over: Something flipped over comes to rest the other way up, so the letters it names are written back to front.

blocks.note: S is small on any clothing label
a fuss is an ADO, turned round

annotation.surface: A minor commotion over a soft drink.
annotation.walkthrough: S for small comes first and stays as it is; it is the fuss that turns. Soda water is what makes a whisky long, and the bracket is there to stop you writing in something stronger.
annotation.definitionFit: Soda is the carbonated water drunk on its own or as a mixer, and it brings no alcohol of its own to the glass.

entries.clue: Commit burglary with mafiosi uptown, in the end I'll sing (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a bird, while 'I'll sing' is a promise in the first person; Everyman lets the robin speak for itself instead of naming the species.

indicatorNotes.in the end: What comes in the end of a word is its final letter, so each word named gives up that letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: to rob a house is to burgle it
the last letters of mafiosi and of uptown

annotation.surface: A burglary with gangsters from the smart end of town, and someone who will eventually talk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'll sing' is the informer's threat on the surface and the bird's own line underneath, and that switch is the step no letter can show you. Uptown is American for the smarter end of a city, which is what keeps the mafia in shot.
annotation.definitionFit: The robin sings through the British winter when almost nothing else does, so the bird can fairly claim the line as its own.

entries.clue: Against church boxing plonk Dutch sold (9)

indicatorNotes.boxing: A boxer's arms close round an opponent, so the letters named before it wrap round the ones named after.

blocks.note: con is the against side of a pro-and-con argument
CE is the Church of England
plonk is British for cheap wine, and vin is the French for wine
D is the dictionary short form for Dutch

annotation.surface: Objections to a church that boxes up cheap wine the Dutch have sold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' is the ring rather than the carton: the pieces named before it part and take the next one inside. Plonk is British for cheap, undistinguished wine, which is what lets a French word answer it.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone sold on an idea has been convinced of it - the sales-floor sense of sold, meaning persuaded rather than traded.

entries.clue: Changing sides in boorish form (5)

indicatorNotes.Changing sides: The sides here are left and right, so changing them trades the letter that stands for one for the letter that stands for the other.

blocks.note: crass is the word for coarse and boorish
the R that sits second in that word is right, and the side it changes to is left

annotation.surface: A defection carried out in a coarse, ill-mannered way.
annotation.walkthrough: R and L are the crossword's right and left, and trading one for the other is all that 'changing sides' asks for. Form is the British school word for a year group - the third form, the sixth form - which is where the definition is hiding.
annotation.definitionFit: In British schools a form is the group a pupil is taught with, and class is the ordinary word for the same group.

entries.clue: Oxford University often admitting a German, Bill - and later another? That's capital! (11)

indicatorNotes.often: Often means many times over, so the two letters it follows are not written once but again and again.
indicatorNotes.admitting: To admit is to let in, so the pieces named next go among the letters already gathered rather than after all of them.

blocks.note: OU is how Oxford University abbreviates itself
the word a, then G for German
a bill pasted on a wall is an advertisement, AD for short
the second of the three
another German, arriving further along
the third and last

annotation.surface: Oxford University repeatedly letting in a German called Bill, and later a second one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' is the poster sense, as in post no bills, which is what makes it an AD. Ouagadougou is the capital of Burkina Faso in West Africa, and OU turns up in it three times over.
annotation.definitionFit: Ouagadougou is the seat of government of Burkina Faso, so capital is the plain geographical sense rather than the Edwardian exclamation the surface wants.

entries.clue: Departures that are listed in charts (1-5)

annotation.definitionNote: Departures answers the six letters without the hyphen the enumeration insists on; the setter is trading on one spelling reading two ways.

blocks.note: an aside steps away from the main line of talk
the A-side is the track a record label pushes, and it is the side that charts

annotation.surface: Departures of some kind written up on a chart.
annotation.walkthrough: A single's A-side is the track the label wants played, and it is the A-side that enters the charts while the B-side rarely does. Read without its hyphen the same six letters spell asides, the remarks made away from the main matter.
annotation.definitionFit: Departures -> ASIDES: an aside departs from the main line of talk; listed in charts -> A-SIDES: the plugged side of a single is the one the charts record.

entries.clue: Groups of performers without safety equipment? (6)

blocks.note: to be without a thing is to have no such thing
the nets strung under a trapeze act

annotation.surface: A trapeze troupe working with nothing strung beneath them.
annotation.walkthrough: A nonet is nine musicians, or the piece written for them, and the word sits in the row with duet, quartet and octet. The question mark marks the trapeze reading as a joke rather than a second definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A nonet is a group of nine performers, or the music scored for nine parts, so the plural names several such groups.
